title: Explore An Artist Through A Live Activity
objective: Take part in a real artist activity and keep a clear record of what you explored.

blocks.text: BUILD · Art · Trinity Arts Award Explore. Explore An Artist Through A Live Activity.
Objective: Take part in a real artist session and keep a clear record of what you explored.
Success evidence: After the real session: the real artist’s identity, the pupil’s own action and finding, and an exact evidence location. Rehearsal stays labelled preparation.
You can explore through looking, listening, asking and trying. Choose a way to take part that works for you. You do not need to share private facts about your life.
We may go to them, they may come in, or we may meet live on screen. The route comes from the current slot card. No meeting is promised by this deck.
40-minute lesson frame. Staff may extend or split the real experience across sessions.

This deck serves Explore Part B, Explore. Part B requires at least one artist AND at least one arts organisation, through live or active experience. Desk research alone fails; archives and prerecorded video are preparation only. Explore has four parts, each a distinct activity. Overall Pass allows ONE Attempted. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. The whole Explore portfolio has a 10-file cap, organised digitally by part. The three assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, and communication. Results are Pass or Below Pass only. Only an adviser trained at Explore may assess; delivery is through a validated centre. Neither local training nor validation is asserted as confirmed here. Advisers must not write plans, reviews or evidence for pupils. Scribe or record the pupil's own words and check them back unchanged. Core, Extend and Challenge are support routes within Explore and retain the live or active requirement. An evidence locator names the filename plus page, slide or timecode. Read the current PRACTITIONER_SLOT and ORG_SLOT from tools/artsaward/SLOTS.json; no candidate name or date is embedded here. R1 pupils visit, R2 the artist or arts organisation comes in, R3 live remote exchange: all remain unconfirmed until actually arranged. Do not treat a recorded video as a live exchange. Source: tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Explore and universal rules. This is the artist-focused Part B deck. It does not remove the separate arts organisation element, which may be evidenced in the same genuine encounter or in the next focused lesson. Read both current slots. Use the classroom models only for rehearsal, never as invented contact with the named artist. When an activity is confirmed, use the lab and independent stages for real participation and accurate capture; extend or split the experience as needed. If none is ready, teach observation and question skills, keep the record as preparation, and arrange the missing real activity. No filming or public posting is required; obtain any needed consent for the chosen evidence format.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Check PRACTITIONER_SLOT and ORG_SLOT, actual readiness and access before selecting the experience or rehearsal route. Keep unconfirmed details blank.

blocks.text: Get ready to notice a choice
Find the question you prepared for an artist. Point to the detail that made you choose it.
Read the current artist card with staff. It tells us which real person and session, if any, are arranged. A blank card means we still need that step.
Keep a place to note the real name later. Do not fill it with a guess or the name of someone from a film.
Think about how you can take part. You might ask or show a detail. You could try a step. Use a way the real session allows.
The arts group also needs to be explored. Today we focus on the artist. We keep that other job in view.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Draw the two loops live and leave them visible. Accept a gesture locating the gap. Do not attach an invented artist identity to this demo.

blocks.text: Rehearsal: a closer look
Watch the adult make a loop on scrap paper. Look at where it starts and where it ends.
Now they make a second loop, with a small gap left open. What changed in the line? Point to the place.
A closer look helps you find something worth asking about. It may be a tool, a shape, a sound or a way to move.
You do not need to decide whether the work is best or worst. Start with what you can notice.
This is a classroom practice. It helps you look closely; it is not a record of contact with the artist in the slot.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Keep the model explicitly labelled rehearsal. During a real exchange, facilitate the pupil’s question and response without answering for the artist or completing the pupil’s task.

blocks.text: Rehearsal model: look, ask and respond
The adult models how a question can grow from what is there. They point to the open loop and ask why a maker might leave a gap.
Next they try a loop of their own. They leave a gap in a new place. They look at what it does to the shape.
The adult names that try as their own response. They do not claim it tells them what an absent artist thinks.
In a real session, use the artist's work or actions as your starting point. Look or listen for a choice you want to explore.
Ask your question in an agreed way. An adult can read your own words. Or you can point to the part you mean.
Give the artist time to respond. Notice a word, a gesture or a step they show. If a try is offered, take part with the safe tools provided.
Keep what you learnt close to that moment. It may differ from what you expected.
If a reply is not clear, ask for a closer view or a simpler step. Finding out can take more than one look.

blocks.title: Explore a real artist through action
blocks.caption: Notice, ask, respond and keep the finding.
blocks.alt: Four linked boxes show noticing a choice, asking a question, responding and keeping a record of what was found.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Answer key: A/C preparation; B/D can evidence real exploration after they actually happen. A live screen is a route, not proof by itself; check the actual exchange.

data.heading: Put a real experience record in order
data.instruction: Put these steps in order for a real artist session. Use each place once. If the session is not ready, this is practice.

items.label: Keep a true note of what you did and found out.
items.feedback: The record follows the action. Name the artist, session and what you actually explored.

items.label: Ask staff if the real session is ready. Check how you will take part.
items.feedback: Readiness comes first. Do not invent an experience while it is still being arranged.

items.label: Respond to what the artist shows or says.
items.feedback: Use the real exchange or activity to notice, try, ask or respond.

items.label: Join the real artist session in the agreed way.
items.feedback: Take part through the agreed route. An old film alone is preparation, not this session.

data.discussion: Tell the adult which step you can really do today. If it is practice time, keep that label and leave the real reply blank.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Capture the pupil’s actual action and finding. Staff observations may describe what occurred but must not invent the pupil’s thoughts. Keep permissions proportionate to the chosen format.

blocks.text: A clear record shows your part
A picture of some tools does not show what you explored. Add the action that belongs to you.
After the real session, record who the artist was and what they did. Then say what you asked, tried, noticed or found out.
Keep those two roles clear. You may have tried a process the artist showed. That does not make their work your own.
Use the real name from the confirmed card or source. Staff can help check spelling. Do not guess that the artist belongs to a group just because both names appear nearby.
Choose evidence that shows the moment. A work sample with a note may help. So may a short clip or a staff note.
Your own finding can be spoken, shown or written. Ask an adult to read back any words they write for you.
Label a practice as practice. An unanswered question stays a question.

boxes.head: BEFORE
boxes.line1: the question I want to ask

boxes.head: AFTER IT HAPPENS
boxes.line1: the artist, my action and finding
boxes.line2: a record of the real experience

blocks.title: A question and an experience record differ
blocks.caption: Record what happened; keep an open question open.
blocks.alt: Two panels contrast a prepared question with a record made after the real artist session, naming the artist, pupil action and finding.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Select the correct branch explicitly. Give the live/active element sufficient time, including across sessions. Absence of an arrangement is not evidence of participation.

blocks.text: Take part when the real session is ready
Staff will say whether the real session is ready or this is practice time. Use the right label.
If it is ready, join in through the agreed route. Keep your question where you can use it. Look, listen and take your part in what the artist offers.
Ask for a pause or a clearer view if needed. Let staff help with tools, sound or space.
If no real session is ready, practise the loop exercise and improve your question. Try saying or pointing it with an adult.
Keep that practice as preparation. Save the place for the real answer until there is one.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Support the same real-experience requirement across tiers. Record the actual date only after the activity; keep organisation claims separate and source-checked.

blocks.text: Keep what you actually found
After a real session, make a record. The details are still fresh. Name the artist and the session accurately.
Show your own action and one thing you found out. Point to a sample or moment that helps explain it.
If only preparation took place, keep that label. Improve your question or note about a detail. Label it clearly and leave the experience record open.
Find the arts group part of your sheet too. Was that group actively explored in this same experience? Check with staff. A name alone does not show that.
Save the record in Part B. Write the filename and page, slide or timecode. Keep preparation and real experience easy to tell apart.

items: Core · keep your question and prompt strip close. Use them to take part in the real artist session. Point, ask through an adult or try with support. Keep who the artist was, what you explored and the file location. If only rehearsed, label it preparation.

Extend · take part in the same real session and make your own record. Link a detail in the artist’s work to your question, try or response. Keep the artist element separate from the arts group element.
Challenge · keep the same real experience and record. Use the artist’s reply to form a follow-up, or try a change they suggest. Explain what that helped you find out. Do not invent an answer.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: Confirm the activity status and locator. Do not complete the full Part B check solely because the artist-focused lesson has ended.

blocks.text: Tell what is known and what is still open
Show staff the detail you chose to keep. Explain or point to what it helped you find out.
Check the label: real artist session, or preparation. If part is still to do, say which part.
Make sure someone can find the evidence from your location note. Fix a page or timecode if it points to the wrong place.
Keep any new question. It may help when you explore the arts group and the way it supports art.

print.intro: Use your question in a real artist session when arranged. Keep the artist’s identity, your own action and what you found. Rehearsal remains preparation.

checks: A real artist is identified from the real source, without a guessed name.
The record distinguishes real live or active work from practice.
My own action and finding are visible, spoken or written.
